stories.headline: Lakewood man arrested on suspicion of murdering wife, a Jefferson County art teacher
stories.summary:
A Lakewood man has been arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder after his wife, a Jefferson County elementary school art teacher, was found dead at their home. Lindsey Barnett, 37, was discovered unresponsive at a residence in the 1700 block of South Welch Circle early Thursday morning, and was pronounced dead on the scene. Her husband, Patrick Theodore Barnett, 40, was arrested following a comprehensive investigation by Lakewood police detectives and is being held in the Jefferson County Jail without bond.

Lindsey Barnett served students at both Hutchinson and Westgate Elementary schools in Jefferson County. School officials remembered her in a letter to the Hutchinson community as a 'sweet soul' with a deep passion for teaching art and an 'extraordinary dedication' to students. The school's principal, DeAnn Hoffman, noted that mental health and district support staff have been made available to help students and staff.

Patrick Barnett is scheduled to appear in court at 10 a.m. on August 20. The case remains under investigation by the Lakewood Police Department.

stories.headline: Pedestrian killed on northbound I-25 near Denver after being struck by pickup truck
stories.summary:
A pedestrian was killed in an early morning crash on northbound Interstate 25 near East 58th Avenue in north Denver on Monday. Colorado State Patrol troopers responded at approximately 5:25 a.m. to the scene near milepost 215, where investigators believe a Chevrolet Silverado lost control and struck a man on the right shoulder of the highway. The impact threw the pedestrian over a concrete barrier, and he landed on a road below and was killed.

The victim's identity was not immediately released and will be determined by the Adams County Coroner's Office. The right lane of northbound I-25 between 48th and 58th avenues remained closed as of 7 a.m. Monday while the crash was investigated. The Colorado State Patrol said the incident remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Aurora police arrest Colorado Springs man in connection with deadly shooting
stories.summary:
Aurora police arrested a 31-year-old Colorado Springs man on Monday in connection with a deadly shooting that occurred in Aurora on Sunday. Armanni Woods was taken into custody by Aurora Police Department's fugitive unit, working alongside the Colorado Springs Police Department's SWAT team. The arrest was announced in a Monday afternoon press release from the Aurora Police Department.

Details of the circumstances surrounding the shooting and the victim were not fully disclosed in the initial release. The arrest marks a quick resolution to the investigation, with the suspect apprehended in Colorado Springs within roughly 24 hours of the incident occurring.

stories.headline: DIA security fence breached six times since 2023, including fatal runway strike in May
stories.summary:
Six individuals have breached Denver International Airport's perimeter fence since September 2023, culminating in the May death of Michael Mott, 41, who scaled the airport's 8-foot barbed-wire fence and was struck and killed by a Frontier Airlines plane accelerating for takeoff. The Denver Post obtained police records detailing the incidents, which include a driver who crashed through a perimeter gate, a man found sitting on an active taxiway, and a man who told police he was trying to walk to Texas. Denver's chief medical examiner ruled Mott's death a suicide.

Aviation security experts say the number of breaches is not immediately alarming and is likely a reflection of improved detection and reporting rather than a surge in incidents. Annmarie Heth, an assistant professor of aviation and aerospace sciences at Metropolitan State University of Denver, noted that advanced technology typically allows security to catch trespassers before serious incidents occur. At least two of the eight trespassers involved across these cases had active arrest warrants at the time of their breach.

DIA officials declined to comment on the trespassing incidents. There is no national database tracking airport perimeter breaches, making direct comparisons with other airports difficult, according to Heth. The report related to the May fatal incident has not yet been released as the case remains under investigation.

stories.headline: Cargill workers in Fort Morgan ratify new contract, ending nearly three-month lockout
stories.summary:
Members of Teamsters Local Union 455 voted Monday to ratify a new five-year contract with Cargill's Fort Morgan beef processing plant, ending a lockout that had kept more than 1,700 workers off the job since May 20. The vote was 1,113 to 211 in favor of the new agreement, with 1,342 total ballots cast. The vote followed a petition from members seeking a revote on Cargill's previous offer.

The approved contract includes the same total wage increase of $2.15 per hour over five years as the earlier rejected offer, but the raises are front-loaded so workers receive more money earlier in the contract period. Bonuses under the new agreement are also higher than those in the original proposal. The dispute had centered on wages, benefits, and workplace protections.

Colorado State Sen. Byron Pelton (R-District 1) commended the agreement while criticizing the negotiating tactics used during the dispute. Pelton noted the lockout placed a significant burden on local families and businesses in the Fort Morgan area and expressed hope that the deal would usher in a 'more constructive relationship' between workers and Cargill management.

stories.headline: Denver reinstates online parking ticket dispute system after nearly a year of in-person-only hearings
stories.summary:
Denver will restore an online parking ticket dispute system beginning September 14 for tickets issued after August 25, reversing a policy that required drivers to appear in person at Denver County Court to contest citations. The change comes roughly a year after the city eliminated parking magistrate positions and shut down the digital dispute portal as part of a broader effort to address a $200 million projected budget shortfall requested by Mayor Mike Johnston. The new system will allow drivers to challenge tickets fewer than 20 days old and will be administered by the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure rather than the court.

The switch to mandatory in-person hearings drew immediate public backlash. The dispute desk was only open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, and hearings were scheduled months out, creating prolonged headaches for drivers contesting tickets ranging from $35 to $250. In-person parking hearings at Denver County Court jumped from 28 in the four months before the change to 464 in the four months after.

Johnston agreed in October 2025 to restore an online option, but implementation took longer than anticipated. City spokesman Jon Ewing acknowledged the frustration the policy caused and said the new system is expected to be 'better than ever.' The Department of Transportation and Infrastructure did not immediately provide additional details about the new platform.

stories.headline: Savannah Bananas deliver measurable economic boost to downtown Denver businesses
stories.summary:
The Savannah Bananas' two sold-out games at Coors Field last weekend generated a significant economic lift for downtown Denver restaurants, hotels, retail shops and entertainment venues. According to data from the Downtown Denver Partnership, the Bananas' 2025 Denver appearance drew more than 215,000 downtown visitors on a single game day, ranking as the fourth-highest visit day of that year. Businesses near Coors Field reported revenue and foot traffic increases of 42 to 75 percent compared to the same weekend in prior years.

This year's two-game Banana Ball World Tour stop again sold out, with some tickets purchased online as early as two months in advance. Local retailers, including permanent jewelry shop Chained Up Charm Bar on Wazee Street, reported that banana-clad fans made up a majority of weekend customers. Several nearby restaurants added banana-themed menu items to capitalize on the visiting crowd.

The Maven Hotel at Dairy Block sold out both game nights and anticipated an 18 percent year-over-year revenue increase for the weekend. The Bananas faced the Indianapolis Clowns in both matchups and were joined on the field by Frozen actress Kristen Bell, who performed live for the crowd. The economic ripple effects stand in contrast to Coors Field's typical Rockies game attendance, which has not produced comparable sellout crowds in recent seasons.

stories.headline: Denver's Five Points jazz club owners to open Parisian-inspired Champagne bar next door
stories.summary:
The owners of Nocturne, the 11-year-old Five Points jazz and supper club, will open a new adjacent bar called La Vie En Rose on September 4. The 1,300-square-foot Parisian-inspired bistro at 1336 27th St. will feature one of the largest Champagne-by-the-bottle lists in Colorado, with 120 selections, alongside cocktails featuring French spirits and a small menu of shareable plates.

Nicole and Scott Mattson are behind the project. The space will include plush seating, velvet curtains, a curved bar with a built-in Champagne bowl, and a climate-controlled wine storage area occupying the full mezzanine level. A small patio will also be available. Hours will run Wednesday through Sunday evenings.

stories.headline: Denver Public Schools board holds daylong retreat to address internal trust breakdown
stories.summary:
All seven members of the Denver Public Schools elected board gathered Monday for a nearly eight-hour retreat aimed at repairing fractured working relationships among directors and with Superintendent Alex Marrero. Using a conversation facilitator, the board engaged in trust-building exercises and frank discussions about transparency, respect, and bureaucratic dysfunction within the board's own processes. The retreat came amid a summer of escalating tensions between board members and the superintendent, who has publicly described their relationship as 'increasingly untenable.'

The three newest directors — Amy Klein Molk, Vice President Monica Hunter, and Treasurer DJ Torres — used the retreat to voice frustrations about board operations. Torres said he has struggled to get items placed on the board's agenda, while Klein Molk said she has had difficulty obtaining data from the district. Hunter said some board members had irreparably violated her trust.

The superintendent's contract was not formally discussed during Monday's retreat, though it has been a source of significant tension. The board met in closed session last month to discuss Marrero's employment, and an attempt earlier this month to schedule a follow-up meeting fell apart for lack of a board majority. Monday's retreat was held at the Denver Police Protective Association Event Center and was open to the public.

stories.headline: Broncos rookie running back Jonah Coleman impresses in preseason debut, drawing praise from Sean Payton
stories.summary:
Rookie running back Jonah Coleman made a strong impression in Denver's preseason opener against Atlanta, logging 14 snaps and prompting head coach Sean Payton to pull him after just four carries — saying he had seen enough evidence of the player's ability. Payton praised Coleman for his balance, elusiveness and short-area quickness, drawing a physical comparison to former NFL standout Maurice Jones-Drew, though stopping short of a formal comp for the young player. Coleman is trending toward earning a role in Denver's running back rotation alongside J.K. Dobbins and RJ Harvey.

On the injury front, wide receiver Jaylen Waddle and center Alex Forsyth returned to practice Monday after missing time. Waddle had been sidelined all of last week with a muscle strain but appeared as a full participant. Tight end Nate Adkins and guard Alex Palczewski also returned.

Inside linebacker Levelle Bailey, who suffered a fracture in his lower leg during Friday's game against Atlanta, faces an uncertain timeline for return. Payton said it was too early to say whether Bailey could return at any point this season. Receiver Marvin Mims Jr. and starting center Luke Wattenberg continued rehabilitation work on the side field.

stories.headline: Tight end Evan Engram says offensive coordinator Davis Webb has built a system for everyone in Broncos offense
stories.summary:
Broncos tight end Evan Engram credits newly elevated offensive coordinator Davis Webb as the primary reason he chose Denver over the Los Angeles Chargers in free agency, citing their shared history as New York Giants teammates and Webb's influence on the offensive scheme. Engram said Webb has built an offense that spreads the ball to multiple weapons, which he expects to make the unit more dangerous when the regular season begins. Engram enters his second season with the Broncos after finishing 2025 with 50 catches for 461 yards and one touchdown.

Engram acknowledged his first year in Denver felt somewhat below expectations but said he addressed what he could control during the offseason before learning Webb would be elevated to play-caller. Head coach Sean Payton has indicated the Broncos plan to use Engram in a wider variety of roles this season, including more frequently as a run blocker rather than primarily a vertical pass threat.

Webb's promotion to offensive coordinator came this spring after Denver finished 14-3, won a playoff game, and came close to a Super Bowl berth. Engram said the new system has produced standout camp performances from multiple receivers, including Courtland Sutton, Troy Franklin, and Pat Bryant.

stories.headline: Broncos close Monday training camp practice to fans after weekend storm damages bleachers
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos closed Monday's training camp practice to fans after severe weekend storms caused wind gusts that shifted temporary bleachers at the team's new facility, raising structural integrity concerns. A Monday afternoon safety inspection found no damage, clearing the way for fans to return Tuesday for what is scheduled as one of the final two open practices of the summer. The bleachers, installed in a new location this season following the opening of the team's new headquarters, can seat approximately 1,000 fans.

The weekend storms dropped between 1.5 and 3 inches of rain across parts of the southeast metro and produced significant hail near the Broncos' facility. Two Cherry Creek School District schools in Aurora were also closed Monday due to flooding caused by the storms. Denver had originally scheduled 14 open training camp practices this summer; Monday's closure brought the total of lost open practices to two, with Tuesday set to be the 11th open session.

Fans are required to have a free ticket to attend open practices. Tuesday's session begins at 10 a.m., with parking lots opening at 8 a.m. and gates at 9 a.m.

topStory.headline: New York State Judge Delays Mangione Murder Trial, Gives Prosecutors Until October to Answer Double Jeopardy Motion
topStory.summary:
A New York state judge on Monday effectively postponed the murder trial of Luigi Mangione, 28, who is accused of fatally shooting UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on Dec. 4, 2024. Justice Gregory Carro, presiding over the state case, ordered prosecutors to respond by Oct. 9 to a defense motion seeking dismissal of the state charges, and set Mangione's next state court appearance for Dec. 10, pushing the trial well past its previously scheduled Sept. 8 start date.

Mangione's defense attorneys filed the 32-page dismissal motion on Friday, one day after he pleaded guilty in federal court to interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death. The defense argued that proceeding with the state case would constitute double jeopardy, characterizing Mangione as a 'pawn in parallel prosecutions.' The Manhattan District Attorney's office, which brought the state charges, declined to comment Monday but said in a Friday statement that it was prepared to litigate the motion and remained 'committed to seeking justice for Mr. Thompson and his family.'

In the state case, Mangione faces charges of second-degree murder, multiple weapons counts and forgery, and has pleaded not guilty. During last week's federal hearing, Mangione admitted to planning and carrying out Thompson's killing, telling the court he was motivated by frustrations with the health insurance system and his own difficulty obtaining treatment for severe back pain. He also revealed that he had posed as an investment manager overseeing more than $50 billion in assets in an email to UnitedHealthcare leadership in order to confirm the location of the investor conference Thompson was attending when he was shot.

Legal experts say the double jeopardy argument faces significant hurdles. New York state's double jeopardy statute is considered more defendant-friendly than federal law, barring successive prosecutions for the same course of conduct, but it includes exceptions when the charges involve substantially different elements or aim to prevent different types of harm. Pace University law professor Bennett Gershman noted that the elements of federal stalking and state murder are 'very, very distinguishable,' since the stalking charges require intent to kill but not that a death actually occur. Prosecutors have indicated they will fight the motion at least until the outcome of Mangione's federal sentencing, which is scheduled for Dec. 18, at which point the Justice Department has said it will seek a life sentence.
